title: ICE-EM Mathematics 8 — Chapter 5: Review of geometry

topics.title: Proving that two lines are parallel

classification.difficultyReason: Apply adjacent-angle, straight-angle and revolution totals to the supplied diagrams, giving reasons.

inlines.text: in each diagram below, giving reasons for your answer. In parts g and j, find the reflex angle

spec.description: Straight line COB and upper-left ray OA.
spec.mathematics: C,O,B are collinear; angle COA is 28 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 28-degree angle is visible.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB+28^\circ&=180^\circ\\\angle AOB&=152^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles in the straight angle $\angle COB$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: OA splits right angle BOC.
spec.mathematics: Angle BOC is 90 degrees and angle AOC is 25 degrees.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB+25^\circ&=90^\circ\\\angle AOB&=65^\circ\end{align*}$$
The adjacent angles form right angle $\angle BOC$.

spec.description: Adjacent angles BON and NOA.
spec.mathematics: Angle BON is 46 degrees; angle NOA is a right angle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied angle and right-angle mark are visible.

answer.worked:
$$\angle AOB=90^\circ+46^\circ=136^\circ$$
Adjacent angles at $O$ can be added.

spec.description: Straight angle XOB divided by OY and OA.
spec.mathematics: Angle XOY is 40 degrees; angle YOA is 112 degrees.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB+112^\circ+40^\circ&=180^\circ\\\angle AOB&=28^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles in the straight angle $\angle XOB$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: Straight line AOB with marked vertex O. The source red point is rendered black under house style.
spec.mathematics: A,O,B lie on a straight line in that order.

answer.worked: $\angle AOB=180^\circ$, because $A$, $O$ and $B$ lie on a straight line.

spec.description: OM lies inside angle BOA.
spec.mathematics: Angle BOM is 105 degrees and angle MOA is 20 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the two givens are labelled.

answer.worked:
$$\angle AOB=20^\circ+105^\circ=125^\circ$$
Adjacent angles at $O$ can be added.

spec.description: Five rays and a curved mark identifying the reflex sector.
spec.mathematics: Successive non-reflex sectors from OA to OB are 33,30,27,24 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Reflex angle is marked but its value is hidden.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{reflex }\angle AOB+33^\circ+30^\circ+27^\circ+24^\circ&=360^\circ\\\text{reflex }\angle AOB&=246^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles in a revolution at $O$ add to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Four rays around O, with right angle BON.
spec.mathematics: Angle BON is 90 degrees; NOM and MOA are each 70 degrees.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB+90^\circ+70^\circ+70^\circ&=360^\circ\\\angle AOB&=130^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles in a revolution at $O$ add to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Straight line BOJ with five upper rays; 5-degree label has an external curved pointer.
spec.mathematics: From OJ towards OA the sectors are 5,15,25,35,45 degrees.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB+45^\circ+35^\circ+25^\circ+15^\circ+5^\circ&=180^\circ\\\angle AOB&=55^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles in the straight angle $\angle BOJ$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: Five rays clockwise from OA to OB; left curved mark selects the reflex angle.
spec.mathematics: Successive sectors are 40,42,44,46 degrees.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{reflex }\angle AOB+40^\circ+42^\circ+44^\circ+46^\circ&=360^\circ\\\text{reflex }\angle AOB&=188^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles in a revolution at $O$ add to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Three distinct rays from O, with external O label and curved pointer. C,O,A are not collinear.
spec.mathematics: Angles COA and BOC are each 165 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: The small angle AOB is unlabelled.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB+165^\circ+165^\circ&=360^\circ\\\angle AOB&=30^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles in a revolution at $O$ add to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Seven rays in clockwise order A,B,C,D,E,F,G.
spec.mathematics: Successive known angles BOC,COD,DOE,EOF,FOG,GOA are 75,65,55,45,35,25 degrees.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB+75^\circ+65^\circ+55^\circ+45^\circ+35^\circ+25^\circ&=360^\circ\\\angle AOB+300^\circ&=360^\circ\\\angle AOB&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles in a revolution at $O$ add to $360^\circ$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–3 form an equation using adjacent angles, a revolution or a straight angle, then calculate the unknown. The geometric-arguments box gives totals of 90 degrees for a right angle, 180 degrees for a straight angle and 360 degrees for a revolution.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Every part asks for an unknown angle with a reason: a,d,i use a straight angle; b uses a right angle; c,f add adjacent angles; e identifies a straight angle; g,h,j,k,l use a revolution. These directly assess unknown-angles-point.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Under Exercise 5A, teacher page 9 starts Question 1 with a 152 degrees (straight angle COB) and b 65 degrees (adjacent angles at O), matching the student diagrams with 28 degrees and 25 degrees respectively. The continuation at the top left of teacher page 10 prints c 136, d 28, e 180, f 125, g 246, h 130, i 55, j 188, k 30 and l 60 degrees. These match, individually, addition of 90+46; subtraction of 40+112 from 180; the straight line AOB; addition of 105+20; subtraction of 33+30+27+24 from 360; subtraction of 90+70+70 from 360; subtraction of 45+35+25+15+5 from 180; subtraction of 40+42+44+46 from 360; subtraction of two 165-degree sectors from 360; and subtraction of 75+65+55+45+35+25 from 360. All twelve independently derived answers agree with the labelled teacher entries and their printed reasons.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify opposite rays at an intersection and name the vertically opposite angle, including intersections within larger figures.

content.prompt: Name the angle that is vertically opposite to $\angle PQR$ in each diagram below.

spec.description: Two straight lines PS and TR intersect at Q. Ordinary source-blue strokes are reconstructed in house black.
spec.mathematics: QP and QS are opposite rays; QR and QT are opposite rays.
spec.answerVisibility: Point labels and both intersecting lines are permanent givens; no answer is shown.

answer.worked: $QP$ and $QS$ are opposite rays, and $QR$ and $QT$ are opposite rays. Therefore $\angle SQT$ is vertically opposite to $\angle PQR$.

spec.description: Lines VP and UR intersect at Q; UR is the steeper line. Ordinary source-blue strokes are reconstructed in house black.
spec.mathematics: QP and QV are opposite rays; QR and QU are opposite rays.
spec.answerVisibility: All point labels and both lines are supplied; no answer is shown.

answer.worked: $QP$ and $QV$ are opposite rays, and $QR$ and $QU$ are opposite rays. Therefore $\angle VQU$ is vertically opposite to $\angle PQR$.

spec.description: Rectangular outline ABPR with diagonals AP and BR meeting at Q; no right-angle markers. Ordinary source-blue strokes are reconstructed in house black.
spec.mathematics: QP and QA are opposite rays; QR and QB are opposite rays.
spec.answerVisibility: Outline, diagonals and vertex labels remain visible; no answer is shown.

answer.worked: $QP$ and $QA$ are opposite rays, and $QR$ and $QB$ are opposite rays. Therefore $\angle AQB$ is vertically opposite to $\angle PQR$.

spec.description: Circle with boundary points P, O, N and R, crossing chords PN and RO, and additional chords RP and ON. Boundary O is distinct from intersection Q. The centre construction coordinate is not drawn or labelled. Ordinary source-blue strokes are reconstructed in house black.
spec.mathematics: QP and QN are opposite rays; QR and QO are opposite rays.
spec.answerVisibility: Circle, all four chords and the five printed point labels are permanent givens; no answer is shown.

answer.worked: $QP$ and $QN$ are opposite rays, and $QR$ and $QO$ are opposite rays. Therefore $\angle NQO$ is vertically opposite to $\angle PQR$.

teachingContext.methodNote: The geometric-arguments summary states that vertically opposite angles are equal. Example 4 identifies opposite angle sectors at intersecting straight lines using their vertex labels.
teachingContext.mappingNote: All four parts assess identifying a vertically opposite angle and expressing its name with Q as the middle letter; no angle calculation is required.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher page's continuation of Exercise 5A prints row 2 as a ∠SQT, b ∠VQU, c ∠AQB and d ∠NQO. Individually comparing the student diagrams: (a) PS and TR cross at Q, making QS and QT opposite to QP and QR; (b) VP and UR cross at Q, giving QV and QU; (c) diagonals AP and BR cross at Q, giving QA and QB; (d) chords PN and RO cross at Q, giving QN and QO. These independently identified angles agree with all four printed answers.

content.prompt: Find the sizes of the angles denoted by $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\theta$ in each diagram below, giving reasons.

spec.description: Two straight lines intersect at B; alpha is opposite the given 56-degree angle.
spec.mathematics: A, B, C are collinear; D, B, E are collinear.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 56-degree angle is shown.

answer.worked: $\alpha=56^\circ$ because vertically opposite angles at $B$ are equal.

spec.description: Intersecting straight lines JKL and MKN with a right-angle square in MKL.
spec.mathematics: MK is perpendicular to KL; theta labels JKM and beta labels JKN.
spec.answerVisibility: The right-angle given is retained; unknown values are hidden.

answer.worked:
$\beta=90^\circ$ (vertically opposite angles at $K$).

$$\begin{align*}\theta+90^\circ&=180^\circ\\\theta&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $JKL$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: Lines AVB and DVC intersect; DVA is 48 degrees, BVC is alpha and DVB is beta.
spec.mathematics: The 48-degree angle is vertically opposite alpha and adjacent to beta.

answer.worked:
$\alpha=48^\circ$ (vertically opposite angles at $V$).

$$\begin{align*}\beta+48^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=132^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $AVB$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: Lines AOC and DOB intersect; OX divides AOB into 28 and 44 degrees.
spec.mathematics: Theta is DOC, vertically opposite AOB.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=28^\circ+44^\circ\\\angle AOB&=72^\circ\\\theta&=72^\circ\end{align*}$$

Adjacent angles are added; vertically opposite angles at $O$ are equal.

spec.description: Three straight lines meet at M, with AMC right, CMF 35 degrees and four unknown sectors.
spec.mathematics: A-M-B, D-M-C and E-M-F are straight lines.
spec.answerVisibility: Right-angle square and 35 degrees are supplied; all unknowns retain Greek labels.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+35^\circ+90^\circ&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=55^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $AMB$ add to $180^\circ$.

$\beta=90^\circ$, $\gamma=35^\circ$ and $\theta=55^\circ$, because each is vertically opposite its corresponding known angle at $M$.

spec.description: Three straight lines meet at O; two upper sectors are each 60 degrees.
spec.mathematics: ROU and FOS are 60 degrees; the remaining sectors are theta, gamma, beta and alpha.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}60^\circ+\theta+60^\circ&=180^\circ\\\theta&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $ROS$ add to $180^\circ$.

$\alpha=60^\circ$, $\beta=60^\circ$ and $\gamma=60^\circ$ by vertically opposite angles at $O$.

spec.description: One connected figure preserves AB, BC, AC, AD, horizontal BMDX and straight CDY, with both intersections and all three numerical givens.
spec.mathematics: At M, DMC is 65 degrees; at D, MDA is 35 degrees and XDC is 160 degrees. Alpha, beta, gamma and theta occupy the original sectors.

answer.short:
$\alpha=65^\circ$, $\beta=115^\circ$, $\gamma=20^\circ$, $\theta=125^\circ$.

Use vertically opposite angles and angles on a straight line at $M$ and $D$.
answer.worked:
$\alpha=65^\circ$ (vertically opposite angles at $M$).

$$\begin{align*}\beta+65^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=115^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $AMC$ add to $180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\gamma+160^\circ&=180^\circ\\\gamma&=20^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $CDY$ add to $180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}35^\circ+\theta+20^\circ&=180^\circ\\\theta&=125^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles above the straight line $MDX$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: Vertical UWD intersects LWR, with a further ray WT in the lower-right sector.
spec.mathematics: LWU is 125 degrees and TWD is 75 degrees; UWR is beta and RWT is alpha.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\beta+125^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=55^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $LWR$ add to $180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}55^\circ+\alpha+75^\circ&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=50^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $UWD$ add to $180^\circ$.

content.prompt: In each diagram below, angles marked with the same Greek letter are equal in size. Find the value of each, giving reasons.

spec.description: Straight lines DVC and BVA intersect; VM divides AVC into two theta-labelled sectors.
spec.mathematics: DVB is 34 degrees; AVM and MVC are equal.

answer.worked:
$\angle AVC=34^\circ$ (vertically opposite angles at $V$).

$$\begin{align*}\theta+\theta&=34^\circ\\2\theta&=34^\circ\\\theta&=17^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Straight JKL with rays KM and KN; the 125-degree angle and two beta sectors fill the upper half-plane.
spec.mathematics: 125 degrees plus twice beta equals 180 degrees.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}125^\circ+\beta+\beta&=180^\circ\\2\beta&=55^\circ\\\beta&=27\tfrac12^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $JKL$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: Three alpha sectors between BA, BD, BE and BC above straight ABC.
spec.mathematics: Three equal angles form a straight angle.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\alpha+\alpha&=180^\circ\\3\alpha&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $ABC$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: Five separate rays VA, VB, VC, VD and VE bound five alpha-labelled sectors.
spec.mathematics: Five equal angles form a revolution. No pair of rays is marked as a straight line.
spec.answerVisibility: All five alpha sectors are unknown.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}5\alpha&=360^\circ\\\alpha&=72^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles in a revolution at $V$ add to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Rays OY, OX and OZ with a right-angle square in YOX and beta on each remaining sector.
spec.mathematics: Two equal beta sectors and a right angle form a revolution.
spec.answerVisibility: The right angle is supplied; beta remains unknown.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\beta+\beta+90^\circ&=360^\circ\\2\beta&=270^\circ\\\beta&=135^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles in a revolution at $O$ add to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Straight EFG and NFM intersect; FP splits NFG into gamma and three gamma. No right-angle square is present.
spec.mathematics: MFG is 45 degrees; EFM is theta; NFP is gamma and PFG is three gamma.
spec.answerVisibility: The given 45 degrees and algebraic labels remain visible; no solved values appear.

answer.short:
$\theta=135^\circ$, $\gamma=33\tfrac34^\circ$.

The angle split into $\gamma$ and $3\gamma$ is vertically opposite $\theta$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\theta+45^\circ&=180^\circ\\\theta&=135^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $EFG$ add to $180^\circ$.

$\angle NFG=135^\circ$ (vertically opposite angles at $F$).

$$\begin{align*}\gamma+3\gamma&=135^\circ\\4\gamma&=135^\circ\\\gamma&=33\tfrac34^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Straight JKL and ray KD, with alpha plus 50 degrees to the left and alpha minus 55 degrees to the right.
spec.mathematics: The two labelled expressions sum to 180 degrees; the source diagram is not to scale.
spec.answerVisibility: Both original algebraic expressions are retained without solved values.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}(\alpha+50^\circ)+(\alpha-55^\circ)&=180^\circ\\2\alpha-5^\circ&=180^\circ\\2\alpha&=185^\circ\\\alpha&=92\tfrac12^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $JKL$ add to $180^\circ$.

spec.description: Straight VWX with upright WB, ray WA, a right-angle square in VWB and labels four alpha and alpha.
spec.mathematics: BWA and AWX together form the remaining right angle.
spec.answerVisibility: The right-angle given and both algebraic labels remain visible.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BWX&=180^\circ-90^\circ\\\angle BWX&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$

Angles on the straight line $VWX$ add to $180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}4\alpha+\alpha&=90^\circ\\5\alpha&=90^\circ\\\alpha&=18^\circ\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
The two marked angles in the diagram are called corresponding angles, because they are in corresponding positions around the two vertices $F$ and $G$.

There are actually four pairs of corresponding angles in the diagram. Can you name the other three pairs?

spec.description: Two unmarked lines AB and CD crossed by PQ at F and G. P is above F and Q below G. A single arc marks PFB and double arcs mark FGD. Source blue ordinary lines are reconstructed in house black.
spec.mathematics: The marked corresponding pair is angle PFB and angle FGD. The other three corresponding pairs occupy the remaining matching positions at F and G. No parallelism is given or required.
spec.answerVisibility: All point labels and both marked sectors are permanent givens; the other three angle pairs appear only in answers.

answer.short: $\angle AFP$ and $\angle CGF$; $\angle AFG$ and $\angle CGQ$; $\angle BFG$ and $\angle DGQ$.
answer.worked:
Match the same position at the two intersections:

Upper left: $\angle AFP$ and $\angle CGF$.

Lower left: $\angle AFG$ and $\angle CGQ$.

Lower right: $\angle BFG$ and $\angle DGQ$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Identify angles in corresponding positions around the two intersections, using the marked upper-right pair as the example.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The task assesses identification of corresponding angle pairs and conventional three-letter angle naming; it does not assess equality or require parallel lines.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The source pixels show the marked pair PFB and FGD. Matching each remaining position gives AFP/CGF, AFG/CGQ and BFG/DGQ. No supplied teacher answer image covers this unnumbered question.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify angle pairs from their positions in twelve diagrams.

content.prompt: In each diagram below, identify each pair of angles marked with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as corresponding angles, alternate angles or co-interior angles.

spec.description: Two gently rising lines crossed by a steep rising transversal; no parallel marks.
spec.mathematics: Alpha and beta are above their respective crossed lines and right of the transversal.

answer.worked: The angles occupy corresponding positions at the two intersections: above each crossed line and on the same side of the transversal.

spec.description: Two descending lines crossed by a gently rising transversal.
spec.mathematics: Alpha and beta are interior angles on opposite sides of the transversal.

answer.worked: The angles lie between the two crossed lines and on opposite sides of the transversal, so they are alternate angles.

spec.description: Two horizontal lines crossed by a rising transversal.
spec.mathematics: Both labelled angles are between the horizontal lines and right of the transversal.

answer.worked: The angles lie between the two crossed lines and on the same side of the transversal, so they are co-interior angles.

spec.description: Two steep descending lines crossed by a gentler descending transversal.
spec.mathematics: Alpha and beta lie inside the steep lines on opposite sides of the transversal.

answer.worked: The angles lie between the two steep lines and on opposite sides of the transversal, so they are alternate angles.

spec.description: Two steep rising lines crossed by a gently rising transversal.
spec.mathematics: Both labelled angles lie between the steep lines and below the transversal.

answer.worked: The angles lie between the two steep lines and on the same side of the transversal, so they are co-interior angles.

spec.description: Two descending lines crossed by a gently rising transversal.
spec.mathematics: Both labels occupy the sector above the transversal between its rightward ray and each line's upper-left ray.

answer.worked: The angles occupy the same relative position at the two intersections, so they are corresponding angles.

spec.description: Unmarked parallelogram-shaped quadrilateral with alpha at upper-left and beta at lower-left.
spec.mathematics: The top and bottom edges are crossed by the left side; both angles are interior and on its right.

answer.worked: Taking the left side as the transversal of the top and bottom edges, both angles lie between those edges and on the same side of the transversal.

spec.description: Parallelogram-shaped quadrilateral with a bottom-left to top-right diagonal.

content.prompt: Find the third angle of a triangle, two of whose angles are given.

answer.worked:
Let the third angle be $x$. The interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}x&=180^{\circ}-(60^{\circ}+30^{\circ})\\x&=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}\\x&=90^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

Let the third angle be $x$. The interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}x&=180^{\circ}-(120^{\circ}+30^{\circ})\\x&=180^{\circ}-150^{\circ}\\x&=30^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

Let the third angle be $x$. The interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}x&=180^{\circ}-(111^{\circ}+11^{\circ})\\x&=180^{\circ}-122^{\circ}\\x&=58^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

Let the third angle be $x$. The interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}x&=180^{\circ}-(62^{\circ}+90^{\circ})\\x&=180^{\circ}-152^{\circ}\\x&=28^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

Let the third angle be $x$. The interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}x&=180^{\circ}-(28^{\circ}+58^{\circ})\\x&=180^{\circ}-86^{\circ}\\x&=94^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

answer.short: Not isosceles: its angles are $38^\circ$, $90^\circ$ and $52^\circ$.

The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. All three angles are different, so no two sides are equal. The triangle is not isosceles.

The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. Since $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$, their opposite sides are equal: $AB=AC$. Hence the triangle is isosceles.

spec.description: Obtuse triangle ABC with C between the unlabelled leftward base extension and B; A is upper left.
spec.mathematics: The exterior angle at C is 72 degrees; the interior angle at B is 36 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the two source angle givens are visible.

answer.worked:
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
$$\begin{align*}\angle CAB+36^\circ&=72^\circ\\\angle CAB&=36^\circ\end{align*}$$
Since $\angle CAB=\angle ABC$, the opposite sides are equal: $BC=AC$. Hence the triangle is isosceles.

spec.description: Left-pointing triangle ABC, A vertically above C; BA extends beyond A.

Angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC&=180^\circ-142^\circ\\\angle BAC&=38^\circ\end{align*}$$
Using the angle sum of a triangle,
$$\begin{align*}\angle BCA&=180^\circ-38^\circ-66^\circ\\\angle BCA&=76^\circ\end{align*}$$
All three angles are different, so the triangle is not isosceles.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with A above and left of C, and BC extended right beyond C.

The exterior angle equals the sum of the opposite interior angles.
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC+37^\circ&=112^\circ\\\angle BAC&=75^\circ\end{align*}$$
All three angles are different, so the triangle is not isosceles.

answer.short:
$\angle ABC=56^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Angles on the straight line $BCD$ add to $180^\circ$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $P$ and $Q$ are points on a circle with centre $O$ such that $\angle POQ=48^\circ$. Draw a diagram and calculate the size of $\angle OPQ$.

answer.short:
$\angle OPQ=66^\circ$.

$OP=OQ$ because they are radii, so the two base angles are equal.
answer.worked:
$OP=OQ$ because they are radii of the same circle. Therefore $\angle OPQ=\angle OQP$ by the base-angle property of an isosceles triangle.
$$\begin{align*}\angle OPQ+\angle OQP&=180^\circ-48^\circ\\\angle OPQ+\angle OQP&=132^\circ\\\angle OPQ&=132^\circ\div2\\\angle OPQ&=66^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Five matching single ticks; collinear C, D, E; exterior alpha at C. The curved 20-degree leader identifies DAE, not BAD.
spec.mathematics: AB=BD=CD=AD=AE; angle DAE=20 degrees.

answer.short:
$\alpha=110^\circ$.

Use the equilateral triangle and then equal base angles.
answer.worked:
$AB=BD=AD$, so $\triangle ABD$ is equilateral and $\angle BDA=60^\circ$.

$AD=AE$, so the base angles of $\triangle ADE$ are equal.

$$\begin{align*}\angle ADE&=(180^\circ-20^\circ)\div2\\\angle ADE&=80^\circ\\\angle CDB&=180^\circ-60^\circ-80^\circ\\\angle CDB&=40^\circ\end{align*}$$

The angles at $D$ lie on a straight line. Since $BD=CD$, the base angles of $\triangle BCD$ are equal.

$$\begin{align*}\angle BCD&=(180^\circ-40^\circ)\div2\\\angle BCD&=70^\circ\\\alpha&=180^\circ-70^\circ\\\alpha&=110^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Rectangular frame, internal isosceles triangle and horizontal CF; all four printed right-angle markers retained.
spec.mathematics: AC=BC; angle ACF=156 degrees; alpha=ABC.

answer.worked:
$AD\parallel CF$ because both are perpendicular to $DE$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle DAC&=180^\circ-156^\circ\\\angle DAC&=24^\circ\\\angle BAC&=90^\circ-24^\circ\\\angle BAC&=66^\circ\end{align*}$$

Co-interior angles give $\angle DAC$; adjacent angles give $\angle BAC$. Since $AC=BC$, the base angles of $\triangle ABC$ are equal, so $\alpha=66^\circ$.

spec.description: Triangle ABC, M on AC, internal BM and three matching double ticks.
spec.mathematics: AM=BM=BC; angle MBC=36 degrees; beta=BAC.

answer.worked:
$BM=BC$, so $\angle BCM=\angle BMC$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle BMC&=(180^\circ-36^\circ)\div2\\\angle BMC&=72^\circ\\\angle AMB&=180^\circ-72^\circ\\\angle AMB&=108^\circ\end{align*}$$

$A,M,C$ are collinear. Since $AM=BM$, the base angles of $\triangle ABM$ are equal.

$$\begin{align*}\beta&=(180^\circ-108^\circ)\div2\\\beta&=36^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Circle with centre O, diameter CB, chords CA and AB, and radius AO.
spec.mathematics: C,O,B collinear; angle ACB=28 degrees; alpha=AOB; beta=ABO.

answer.worked:
$OA=OC$ because they are radii, so $\angle OAC=\angle ACO=28^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle AOC&=180^\circ-28^\circ-28^\circ\\\angle AOC&=124^\circ\\\alpha&=180^\circ-124^\circ\\\alpha&=56^\circ\end{align*}$$

$C,O,B$ lie on a straight line. Also $OA=OB$ because they are radii, so the base angles of $\triangle AOB$ are equal.

$$\begin{align*}\beta&=(180^\circ-56^\circ)\div2\\\beta&=62^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Intersecting AD and BC with E at their intersection; three matching single ticks and leader identifying AEC.
spec.mathematics: AB=AC=CD; angle ABC=43 degrees; angle AEC=106 degrees; beta=ADC.

answer.worked:
$AB=AC$, so $\angle ACE=\angle ACB=43^\circ$ by equal base angles of $\triangle ABC$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle CAE&=180^\circ-106^\circ-43^\circ\\\angle CAE&=31^\circ\end{align*}$$

Since $A,E,D$ are collinear, $\angle CAD=31^\circ$. Since $AC=CD$, the base angles of $\triangle ACD$ are equal, so $\beta=\angle CAD=31^\circ$.

spec.description: Unshaded outer hexagon with red dashed equilateral triangle ABC, upward extension of BA and extension of CA beyond A. Ordinary outline, labels and equality ticks are black.
spec.mathematics: AB=AC=BC; AD=DC; angle ADC=120 degrees; alpha is between upward BA and AD.

answer.worked:
$AB=AC=BC$, so $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\angle BAC=60^\circ$.

$AD=DC$, so the base angles of $\triangle ADC$ are equal.

$$\begin{align*}\angle DAC&=(180^\circ-120^\circ)\div2\\\angle DAC&=30^\circ\\\angle BAD&=60^\circ+30^\circ\\\angle BAD&=90^\circ\\\alpha&=180^\circ-90^\circ\\\alpha&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$

The last step uses adjacent angles on the straight line through $B$ and $A$.

spec.description: Two arms from a vertex meet two parallel shallow rays.

answer.worked:
The smaller angle at the left vertex is $360^\circ-282^\circ=78^\circ$. Draw a ray through that vertex parallel to the marked rays. Corresponding angles divide the $78^\circ$ angle into $52^\circ$ and $\alpha$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=78^\circ-52^\circ\\\alpha&=26^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Three parallel rising lines crossed by shallow and steep descending transversals.
spec.mathematics: Shallow transversal has corresponding obtuse angles 126 degrees and alpha; steep transversal has an obtuse 143-degree angle and lower acute beta.

answer.worked:
Corresponding angles on the shallow transversal give $\alpha=126^\circ$. On the steep transversal, the angle corresponding to $\beta$ is supplementary to $143^\circ$.

spec.description: Two triangles share an intermediate vertex on a straight side; upper-left segment and lower base are parallel.
spec.mathematics: Left exterior angle 158 degrees, top reflex 286 degrees, intermediate lower-left angle 42 degrees; lower triangle unknowns alpha and beta.

answer.short:
$\alpha=106^\circ$, $\beta=20^\circ$

Use the parallel sides and the angle sums of the two triangles.
answer.worked:
The top interior angle is $360^\circ-286^\circ=74^\circ$. Co-interior angles on the marked parallels give
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-74^\circ\\\alpha&=106^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The upper-left triangle has left angle $180^\circ-158^\circ=22^\circ$, so its angle at the intermediate vertex is $180^\circ-74^\circ-22^\circ=84^\circ$. The angle at that vertex in the lower triangle is $180^\circ-84^\circ-42^\circ=54^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=180^\circ-106^\circ-54^\circ\\\beta&=20^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Hexagon with two red dashed intersecting interior segments and one pair of marked parallel outer sides.
spec.mathematics: Left reflex 240 degrees; right upper angle 80 degrees; repeated beta labels above the horizontal dashed segment; alpha below left and gamma at bottom-left.

answer.worked:
Alternate angles on the marked parallel sides give $\alpha=80^\circ$. The whole interior angle at the left vertex is $360^\circ-240^\circ=120^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=120^\circ-80^\circ\\\beta&=40^\circ\end{align*}$$
The lower triangle has an angle of $40^\circ$ at the dashed intersection, vertically opposite the marked $\beta$.
$$\begin{align*}\gamma&=180^\circ-80^\circ-40^\circ\\\gamma&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Perpendicular horizontal and vertical segments with a sloping segment from bottom-left to the top edge.
spec.mathematics: Four supplied right-angle marks; 21 degrees between the left vertical and slope; alpha below top on right of slope and beta above lower internal horizontal.

answer.worked:
The horizontal segments are parallel because each is perpendicular to the vertical sides. The acute angle between the slope and a horizontal is $90^\circ-21^\circ=69^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=69^\circ\\\alpha&=180^\circ-69^\circ\\\alpha&=111^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Rectangular-looking unmarked outline with two red dashed diagonals and four identical half-diagonal ticks. No right-angle or parallel marks are added.
spec.mathematics: All four half-diagonals are equal. Top-right angle between top edge and diagonal is 38 degrees; alpha is the left central angle, beta the upper central angle, gamma the top-left angle beside the left edge.
spec.answerVisibility: Only original marks, givens and unknown labels.

answer.short:
$\alpha=76^\circ$, $\beta=104^\circ$, $\gamma=52^\circ$

Use the equal half-diagonals to identify isosceles triangles.
answer.worked:
The upper triangle has equal sides from the diagonal intersection to the top corners, so both base angles are $38^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\beta+38^\circ+38^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=104^\circ\end{align*}$$
At the intersection, adjacent angles form a straight angle.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+104^\circ&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=76^\circ\end{align*}$$
The left triangle also has equal sides from the intersection to its two corners, so its base angles are both $\gamma$.
$$\begin{align*}\gamma+\gamma+76^\circ&=180^\circ\\2\gamma&=104^\circ\\\gamma&=52^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Irregular quadrilateral with all four interior angles expressed as multiples of alpha.
spec.mathematics: Angles in source order from bottom left: alpha, 4 alpha, 3 alpha, 2 alpha.

answer.worked:
The interior angles of a quadrilateral add to $360^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+4\alpha+3\alpha+2\alpha&=360^\circ\\10\alpha&=360^\circ\\\alpha&=36^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Parallelogram with single arrows on the vertical sides and double arrows on the sloping sides; reflex angle outside the lower-left vertex.
spec.mathematics: Reflex angle 230 degrees and interior alpha at lower left; beta at upper left and gamma at upper right.

answer.worked:
Angles in a revolution add to $360^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+230^\circ&=360^\circ\\\alpha&=130^\circ\end{align*}$$
Co-interior angles between the parallel sloping sides add to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\beta+130^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=50^\circ\end{align*}$$
Co-interior angles between the parallel vertical sides add to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\gamma+50^\circ&=180^\circ\\\gamma&=130^\circ\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The point $O$ is the centre of the circle. Find $\alpha$ in terms of $\beta$.

spec.description: Circle with centre O, a top circumference vertex, two lower circumference vertices, two chords from the top vertex and radii to the lower vertices. No lower chord or top radius is supplied.
spec.mathematics: Beta is the angle at the top circumference point. Alpha is the lower central angle between the two supplied radii.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the source givens are visible.

answer.short:
$\alpha=2\beta$.

Join the top vertex to $O$ and use the two isosceles triangles.
answer.worked:
Call the top vertex $A$, the lower-left vertex $B$ and the lower-right vertex $C$. Join $OA$. Let $\angle BAO=x$ and $\angle OAC=y$, so $x+y=\beta$.

Since $OA=OB=OC$ are radii, the base angles in each of $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle AOC$ are equal. By the triangle angle sum,
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=180^\circ-2x\\\angle AOC&=180^\circ-2y.\end{align*}$$
Angles around $O$ add to $360^\circ$:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=360^\circ-(180^\circ-2x)-(180^\circ-2y)\\\alpha&=2(x+y)\\\alpha&=2\beta.\end{align*}$$

Draw non-crossing internal diagonals to divide the twelve-sided polygon into 10 triangles. All four inward corners remain on its boundary.
$$\begin{align*}S&=10\times180^\circ\\S&=1800^\circ.\end{align*}$$

answer.short: $S=(n-2)\times180^\circ$, where $n$ is the number of sides.
answer.worked:
A polygon with $n$ sides can be divided into $n-2$ triangles by non-crossing internal diagonals. Each triangle contributes $180^\circ$, so the sum of the internal angles is
$$S=(n-2)\times180^\circ.$$

content.prompt: Name all the isosceles triangles in the diagram below.

spec.description: Upright triangle AFG with side points A,H,B,K,F and A,I,C,L,G in order. Segments DI and HE intersect at J; BC is parallel to FG. Exterior triangles DBK and ECL have the four source alpha labels; the base angles of AFG have beta labels. Ordinary source blue strokes are rendered black under house style.
spec.mathematics: D,B,J,I are collinear; H,J,C,E are collinear. BC is parallel to FG. Angles BDK, DKB, CEL and ELC equal alpha. Angles AFG and AGF equal beta. Coordinates provide an unmeasured schematic consistent with these relations.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry, labels, parallel marks and alpha/beta givens are visible.

answer.worked:
The marked equal angles show that $\triangle AFG$, $\triangle BDK$ and $\triangle CEL$ are isosceles.

Since $BC\parallel FG$, corresponding angles give $\angle ABC=\angle BCA=\beta$, so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.

The angle sums of $\triangle BDK$ and $\triangle CEL$ give
$$\angle DBK=\angle ECL=180^\circ-2\alpha.$$
Vertically opposite angles therefore give
$$\angle JBH=\angle JCI=180^\circ-2\alpha.$$
Subtracting these from the equal base angles of $\triangle ABC$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\angle JBC&=\beta-(180^\circ-2\alpha)\\&=2\alpha+\beta-180^\circ,\\\angle JCB&=\beta-(180^\circ-2\alpha)\\&=2\alpha+\beta-180^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle JBC$ is isosceles.

The five triangles established as isosceles are $\triangle AFG$, $\triangle ABC$, $\triangle BDK$, $\triangle CEL$ and $\triangle JBC$. The givens do not establish that $\triangle JBH$ or $\triangle JCI$ is isosceles.

content.prompt: Consider the isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB=AC$. Suppose $D$ is on $AB$ and $E$ is on $AC$, so that $AD=DE$. If $\angle CED=142^\circ$, calculate $\angle ABC$.

inlines.text: Use the straight angle at E, then the equal base angles in triangles ADE and ABC.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AED&=180^\circ-142^\circ\\\angle AED&=38^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles on the straight line $AEC$ add to $180^\circ$.

$AD=DE$, so the base angles of isosceles triangle $ADE$ are equal:
$$\angle DAE=\angle AED=38^\circ.$$
Since $D$ is on $AB$ and $E$ is on $AC$, $\angle BAC=\angle DAE=38^\circ$.

$AB=AC$, so $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$. Using the angle sum of triangle $ABC$,
$$\begin{align*}2\angle ABC+38^\circ&=180^\circ\\2\angle ABC&=142^\circ\\\angle ABC&=71^\circ.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Use angles on a straight line, equal base angles opposite equal sides, and the triangle angle sum. Pages 23–25 establish the isosceles properties; pages 18–19 establish the triangle angle sum; page 2 supplies straight-angle reasoning.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The task combines the equal base angles of ADE with the equal base angles of ABC through their shared apex angle, directly assessing unknown angles in related figures.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The answer image's Challenge exercise item 6 prints angle ABC = 71 degrees. The student item 6 specifies AB = AC, AD = DE and angle CED = 142 degrees. Independent straight-angle and isosceles-triangle reasoning gives angle AED = angle DAE = 38 degrees, then angle ABC = (180 - 38)/2 = 71 degrees.

content.prompt: $ABCD$ is a square and $AEB$ is an equilateral triangle. Calculate the two possible values of the size of $\angle DEC$.

inlines.text: Place the equilateral triangle on each side of AB and use the equal base angles of triangles ADE and BCE.

answer.worked:
Draw square $ABCD$ with vertices in order, then consider the two possible positions of $E$. Join $DE$ and $CE$.

Since $AD=AB=AE$ and $BC=AB=BE$, triangles $ADE$ and $BCE$ are isosceles. Also, $\angle AEB=60^\circ$.

When $E$ is inside the square:
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAE=\angle CBE&=90^\circ-60^\circ\\\angle DAE=\angle CBE&=30^\circ\\\angle AED=\angle BEC&=\frac{180^\circ-30^\circ}{2}\\\angle AED=\angle BEC&=75^\circ\\\angle DEC&=360^\circ-60^\circ-75^\circ-75^\circ\\\angle DEC&=150^\circ\end{align*}$$
The final subtraction uses angles in a revolution at $E$.

When $E$ is on the opposite side of $AB$ from the square:
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAE=\angle CBE&=90^\circ+60^\circ\\\angle DAE=\angle CBE&=150^\circ\\\angle AED=\angle BEC&=\frac{180^\circ-150^\circ}{2}\\\angle AED=\angle BEC&=15^\circ\\\angle DEC&=60^\circ-15^\circ-15^\circ\\\angle DEC&=30^\circ\end{align*}$$
Here $ED$ and $EC$ lie inside $\angle AEB$, so adjacent angles give the final subtraction.

teachingContext.methodNote: Use adjacent angles and angles in a revolution from page 2, the triangle angle sum from pages 18–19, and equal base angles and 60-degree equilateral angles from pages 23–25. Page 25 models concise angle calculations with geometric reasons.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The task combines these taught properties in two configurations of a square and an equilateral triangle; finding unknown angles in figures is the closest directly assessed skill.

content.prompt: Find the value of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ in the diagram below.

spec.description: Scalene triangle ABC, with CB extended beyond B, AC extended beyond C and BA extended beyond A. Exterior labels alpha, beta and gamma occur at B, C and A respectively. Source blue strokes become ordinary black house-style geometry. No angle arcs, numerical values or equality marks are added.
spec.mathematics: One exterior angle at each vertex; each forms a straight angle with its adjacent interior angle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source point names, exterior-angle symbols and side extensions are visible.

inlines.text: Subtract the triangle’s interior angle sum from three straight angles.

answer.worked:
Each labelled exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle add to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=3\times180^\circ-(\angle ABC+\angle BCA+\angle CAB)\\\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=540^\circ-180^\circ\\\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=360^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The interior angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Page 2 states that angles in a straight angle add to 180°. Pages 18–19 establish the triangle interior angle sum and define exterior angles.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Each labelled angle is supplementary to one interior angle. Summing these three relationships and using the triangle angle sum gives the requested total.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image’s Challenge exercise row lists question 8 as 360°. The student question asks for the sum of the three exterior angles alpha, beta and gamma. Independently summing three supplementary relationships and subtracting the triangle’s 180° interior sum gives 360°, agreeing with that entry.

entries.description: The word geometry comes from two Greek words meaning ‘earth measurement’. Its name explains the origin of the subject. In ancient Egypt, the river Nile regularly overflowed its banks and washed away boundary markers between neighbouring properties. The boundaries had to be found again and this led to the study of the different shapes and sizes of triangles.

entries.description:
The following can be used in arguments:
– Adjacent angles can be added.
– Angles in a revolution add to 360°.
– Angles in a straight angle add to 180°.
– Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Two lines are called perpendicular if they meet at right angles.
The Greek letters α (alpha), β (beta), γ (gamma) and θ (theta) are often used as pronumerals to represent angle size in geometry.

entries.description:
Proving that two lines are parallel
Suppose that a transversal crosses two other lines.
• If the corresponding angles are equal, then the lines are parallel.
• If the alternate angles are equal, then the lines are parallel.
• If the co-interior angles are supplementary, then the lines are parallel.

entries.sourceLabel: Proving the theorem about the angle sum of a triangle
entries.description:
We proved last year that the sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°. As we discussed then, checking a theorem many times doesn’t prove it – however many triangles you check, there are always more to check. Here is a totally convincing proof that applies to every triangle, whatever its shape.
The theorem and its proof are set out very formally in the manner traditional for geometry. The proof uses only the methods we have already developed about angles at a point and across transversals.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching introduction; reference evidence only.

entries.description:
Theorem: The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°.
Proof: Let ABC be a triangle.
Let ∠BAC = α, ∠ABC = β and ∠ACB = γ.
We must prove that α + β + γ = 180°.
Draw the line XY parallel to BC and passing through the vertex A.
Then ∠XAB = β (alternate angles, XY ∥ BC),
and ∠YAC = γ (alternate angles, XY ∥ BC).
Hence, α + β + γ = 180° (straight angle ∠XAY).
entries.presentation: Formal theorem and proof with labels in a left gutter; associated diagram on the right.
entries.exclusionReason: Supplied theorem and complete proof, not a student question. Taught method: construct a parallel through the opposite vertex, transfer alternate angles, and use a straight angle.

entries.sourceLabel: The exterior angles of a triangle
entries.description:
Let ABC be a triangle, with the side BC produced to D. (The word ‘produced’ means ‘extended’.) Then the angle ∠ACD between the side AC and the extension CD is called an exterior angle of the triangle.
The angles ∠CAB and ∠ABC are called the opposite interior angles, because they are opposite the exterior angle at the vertex C.

Proof: Let ABC be a triangle, with BC produced to D.

entries.description:
An isosceles triangle is a triangle in which two (or more) sides have equal length.
• The equal sides AB and AC in the isosceles triangle ABC to the right are called the legs. They have been marked with double dashes to indicate that they are equal in length.
• The vertex A where the legs meet is called the apex.
• The third side BC is called the base.
• The angles ∠ABC and ∠ACB at the base are called base angles.
The word isosceles is a Greek word meaning ‘equal legs’ – iso means ‘equal’, and sceles means ‘legs’.

entries.sourceLabel: Isosceles triangles and their base angles
entries.description:
Last year, in Chapter 13 of ICE-EM Mathematics Year 7 we developed in an informal way two results about isosceles triangles. The first is a property that all isosceles triangles have.
• The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
(This result can also be stated as ‘If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the angles opposite those sides are equal.’)
The second is a test for a triangle to be isosceles, and is the converse of the first result.
• If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite those angles are equal.
In Chapter 12 we will introduce congruence, which will allow us to prove these theorems properly.

entries.description:
Theorem: The interior angles of an equilateral triangle are all 60°.
Proof: Let ABC be an equilateral triangle.
Let ∠BAC = α, ∠ABC = β and ∠ACB = γ.
We must prove that α = β = γ = 60°.
β = γ (opposite sides AC and AB are equal), and β = α (opposite sides AC and BC are equal), so α = β = γ.
But α + β + γ = 180° (angle sum of ∠ABC), so α = β = γ = 60°.

entries.description:
We must prove that ∠ABC + ∠BCD + ∠CDA + ∠DAB = 360°.
Join the diagonal AC.
The interior angles of △ABC add to 180°.
Similarly, the interior angles of △ADC add to 180°.
But the sum of the interior angles of ABCD is the sum of the angles of △ABC and △ADC.
Hence, the interior angles of ABCD add to 360°.
